subject: RN model to estimate abundance per site

messages.author: af2b16d60afe57cd
messages.subject: RN model to estimate abundance per site
parts:
Dear all,

 

I´m new to unmark and I tried to calculate the abundance based on Royle-Nichols models. I´m not interested in finding the effect of the variable per se on the abundance of a particular spp (at least not at this point). What I want is to have a better estimate of species abundance per site accounting for imperfect detection. I´m exploring this model as a way to avoid using just raw counts or frequencies for each species (in my case camera trap data, so #independent pics/sample effort*100). I have 56 sites, 33 in habitat type A and 23 habitat type B (here habitat).

 

So, I used M1 <-occuRN(~habitat~1, data.umf) and after I transform (backTransform(M1, type="state"), I have the value of lambda, but this is basically the average abundance for all sites, right? (please confirm in case my interpretation is wrong). As mentioned, I´m not interested in the abundance for the whole landscape (56 sites or per each of both habitats). I´m more interested in having the relative abundance (accounting for p) for each site. So I also tried, “sites” as a factor (model M2 <-occuRN(~sites~1, data.umf), but I get a message saying that there are too many variables. This seems sensible as there would be only one site per each “factor level”, so difficult to do something…


In another attempt, I used ranef(M1) to extract a single estimate of abundance for each site. Could you please confirm if this is correct? or I should be aware of something else? 

The result is something like (for one species, I would need to do this for 26!)


          Mean        Mode  2.5% 97.5%

 [1,] 3.2295318    3          1     6        (this CI seems very high, isn´t it?)

 [2,] 3.2295318    3          1     6

 [3,] 3.2295318    3          1     6

 [4,] 0.6491656    0          0     3....(and so on for 56 sites)   [the values in terms of counts or independent pictures for these 4 sites were in order: 6, 5, 7, 0 !! much higher than the ranef output


So, can I use for sure this "Mode" column as the single estimate of abundance accounting for detection probability given the habitat? 


what would be the usefulness of Predict(M3,type="det") in my case, then? it is giving me the same value for a bunch of sites (~200)

 

I would be very grateful if anybody has any thoughts on this. I know using relative abundance is questionable nowadays and I´m wondering whether this approach could suit my aim, there should not be differences in p between occasions (8), though (not much within sites in each habitat either; one is a monoculture…)… I have actually analyzed everything using a multivariate version of GLM (mvabund package), but have received the suggestion to try to include detection probabilities, so I´m exploring alternatives. 

 

I really appreciate your help! Thanks.

Cheers

 

Lain

messages.author: ca3e0d1feca30c8c
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] RN model to estimate abundance per site
parts:
Hi Lain,

before I get into the issue of camera traps and estimating abundance, here a few points:

backTransform (and predict with "state") give you the mean abundance based on the covariates in the model. Since you have no occupancy covariates the estimates will be the same for all of your sites. ranef() gives site-specific estimates using the data AND the parameter estimates (which in your case assumes no difference across all sites). Now I am not quite sure why you are interested in site specific estimates but not in the effect of covariates on the abundance (e.g. habitat type). It would not make much sense to compare those estimates in a second step for the two habitats, in that case you should model the covariates directly in the occupancy model.

Now there is a larger issue with estimating "abundance" using a RN occupancy model and camera traps. Camera traps are point samples that are not associated with a specific area. There is therefore no way to translate these "abundance" values into density values and not even a clear way to interpret them. Let's assume that you get abundance estimates of 2 for jaguar and 2 for tapir for a specific station. That would mean that the camera is included in the home range of 2 jaguars and 2 tapirs. Now jaguars have home ranges of several 100 km2 while tapirs have home ranges of maybe 2-5 km2 so even though you get the same "abundance" estimates the densities of the two species are hugely different. This means that there is no way to compare abundance estimates across species.

Things get even more complicated when you consider animal movement. Assume you place tow cameras in an animals home range. One close to the home range center (where the animal spends a lot of time) and one closer to the home range edge (where the animal spends less time). The camera in the home range center would get a much larger number of images than the camera at the edge and the RN model would interpreter that as a higher "abundance" even though there is just one animal in both cameras. We have observed this regularly with species such as agouti, paca or deer.

I personally think that the RN model is useful with camera trap data exactly because it improves occupancy estimates when there is the kind of heterogeneity just described that can not be modeled with covariates. You could probably (with some caution) also interpret "abundance" as intensity of habitat use when comparing different habitat types or other covariates, but you can again not compare across species. Occupancy models are a useful tool exactly when you have covariates you want to model but they give you little information in the absence of covariates.

If you want to estimate true abundance you might want to take a look at a recent paper by Howe.

Howe, E. J., Buckland, S. T., Després-Einspenner, M.-L. and Kühl, H. S. (2017), Distance sampling with camera traps. Methods Ecol Evol. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12790

Best,

Mathias

messages.author: af2b16d60afe57cd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] RN model to estimate abundance per site
parts:
Dear Mathias,


Thank you very much for your feedback, I agree with you. And yes, there was no covariate for sites in this model, so estimates would be the same! (that was a silly question, sorry). I understand your point that there is no much sense not to use covariates along with the estimations of abundance/occ. To examine the effect of the covariates on mammalian community composition, I used the mvabund  R package(see Warton et al 2015 and Wang et al 2016). I actually have my analysis done. However, I have received a recommendation to explore alternatives accounting for detection probabilities, so I´m exploring these. The mvabund approach has the advantage that you can analyze all the covariates and all the species simultaneously, so you don´t have to do this one by one (and is better than common multivariate approaches). I will try to use the covariates within this approach in unmarked anyways and compare. Thanks.


My research design was thought for richness and occupancy estimation of the assemblage, not for density or true abundance for a particular species, strictly speaking. However, it is always good to analyze some kind “relative abundance” (composition, frequency, intensity of hab use) along with the richness... But, I was not interested in true abundances/densities, and therefore my design is not suitable for this (at least not for all the species). It seems that the fact that some species abundance estimations, using ranef(), have large CI (with or without covariates) could be a good argument to probably keep my analysis as it is (using independent pictures and frequencies), but further thoughts would be great to consider. I´ll keep exploring this occRN framework and compare with my previous analysis.


Just a final question, it seems that this occRN model is not good for common species, is this a general recommendation?


Thanks much again for these useful observations.


Best

Lain
